text: Johanne Mathilde Dietrichson was the first Norwegian woman to receive a formal art education. Born in Christiania, she grew up in Trondheim and Kongsberg and took a drawing class in Christiania. On the advice of Camilla Collett and Adolph Tidemand she went to Düsseldorf in 1857, where she worked in Otto Mengelberg's studio until 1861. The following year she married the art historian Lorentz Dietrichson and went with him on his travels, living in Rome and then in Stockholm, where she attended the Royal Academy. She painted, and she also made sculptures and ceramics.

John Richardson Jackson learned line engraving from Robert Graves and then took up mezzotint. He was born in Portsmouth, the second son of a banker. He concentrated on portraits, and he engraved numerous ones after George Richmond. In 1847 he engraved The Otter and Salmon after Edwin Landseer, which brought his work to public attention. He also engraved Queen Victoria after William Fowler and The Princess Royal and her Sisters after Franz Xaver Winterhalter. He died at Southsea in 1877.

Kaspar Karsen specialised in townscapes. Born in Amsterdam, he studied with Hendrik Gerrit ten Cate, Dirck Vettewinkel and George Pieter Westenberg. He became a member of the society Arti et Amicitiae in 1836 and enjoyed making trips to Prague and Germany. His pupils included Cornelis Springer and his own son Eduard Karsen. He died in Biebrich near Wiesbaden at the age of 86.

The Paris firm Léon & Lévy took the initials LL as its trademark and specialised in stereoscopic views and picture postcards of places in Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. Isaac Lévy and his son-in-law Moyse Léon founded it in 1864. It was one of the most important postcard editors in France. When Lévy's two sons took over in 1895, they renamed the company Lévy Fils et Cie. Around 1920 the printer Émile Crété bought it and combined it with the firm of Neurdein Frères.

The Master of the Life of the Virgin is the name given to a German painter working in Cologne from about 1463 to 1490. He is also called the Master of Wilten, or identified with Johann van Duyren, which not everyone accepts. His workshop is known for a series of eight scenes from the Life of the Virgin Mary, painted for the Ursulakirche in Cologne. Seven are in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich and one is in the National Gallery in London. The National Gallery also has the four outer panels of an altarpiece from Werden.

Mathilde Weil worked as an editor and reader at Macmillan from 1893 to 1896 and was sub-editor of the American Historical Review. She came from Philadelphia, where her father was a lawyer, and her parents were Jewish. She graduated from Bryn Mawr College in 1892 and studied further at the Philadelphia Museum of Industrial Art and Textile School. She also took a summer course with the painter Joseph DeCamp. She later worked as a literary agent and portrait photographer in Philadelphia.

Morton Livingston Schamberg was one of the first American artists to explore the aesthetic qualities of industrial subjects. He is considered a pioneer of Precisionism and one of the first American adopters of the Cubist style. He was born in Philadelphia, the youngest child in a German Jewish family, and his father was a cattle dealer. He earned a degree in architecture from the University of Pennsylvania in 1903. In 1902 he had discovered an interest in art in a class taught by William Merritt Chase in the Netherlands. He worked as a painter and photographer.

As director of the French Academy in Rome from 1724 until his death, Nicolas Vleughels helped the exchange between France and Italy in the first third of the 18th century. He was born in Paris, the son of the Flemish painter Philippe Vleughels, who had emigrated from Antwerp. He is said to have studied with Pierre Mignard, and he often copied Rubens. He won only the second prize of the Académie royale in 1694, so he had to pay for his own trip to Rome. He was likely in Rome from 1703.

Tomás Yepes painted still lifes and bodegones, pictures of pantry items, in the Kingdom of Valencia. His activity began in the second decade of the 17th century, but most works attributed to him come after 1642. He painted for clients and for public events. His flower vases, fruits, particularly grapes, and everyday objects were prominent in the region, and he has been regarded as one of the major rediscoveries of art history. He is best known for his distinctive style of flower painting.

Vincent Courdouan specialised in marine art. His father was a farrier and veterinarian. At twelve he began his artistic studies with the local artist Pierre Letuaire, and later he spent some time at a small school of naval art under the naval sculptor Jacques-Félix Brun. In 1829 he went to Paris to study engraving and worked in the studio of the painter Paulin Guérin, who also came from Toulon. In 1833 he became a member of the Académie du Var.

Paul Güssfeldt led the first expedition of the German African Society in 1872, which was shipwrecked near Freetown and lost all its stores and equipment. He still set up a station on the coast of Loango but could not reach the interior, and he returned to Germany in 1875. He was born and died in Berlin. He studied natural sciences and mathematics, first in Heidelberg and later in Berlin and Bonn. He was a geologist, mountaineer and explorer.

Ryusai Shigeharu was one of a select group of kamigata-e print artists who could support themselves solely as professional artists. He was an Osaka-based ukiyo-e artist. He was born Yamaguchi Yasuhide in Hizen Province in 1802, and his father ran a money-changing business. Around 1820 he moved to Osaka to study printmaking with his first mentor, and his next teacher collaborated with him on several major projects. Some have suggested he studied under Hokusai, but there is no definitive evidence.

Walenty Wańkowicz is honoured in Belarus as one of the most important 19th-century painters of Belarusian origin, and a monument to him stands in Minsk. His family's former mansion in the historic part of Minsk is now a museum. He studied at the Jesuit College in Polotsk, the University of Wilno and the Imperial Academy of Arts in St Petersburg. He painted a well-known portrait of the poet Adam Mickiewicz. He died in Paris at 43.

Adriaen van Salm mostly made marine art, drawn in pen with India ink on cloth or a prepared panel. He was born in Delfshaven, and in 1706 he was listed as a draughtsman member of the Guild of Saint Luke in Delft. The Dordrechts Museum adds that he was also a schoolmaster and later a draper. He was the father and teacher of Roelof van Salm, who used the same technique and painted especially ships and naval battles. Abraham Jacob van der Aa saw a painting by Adriaen in the collection of the marine painter Johannes Christiaan Schotel.

Aleksandrs Apsītis was born in Riga into a blacksmith's family. After taking lessons in Saint Petersburg, he moved to New Athos, where he illustrated books about the monastery. In 1901 he returned to Saint Petersburg and began illustrating magazines and creating advertising posters. In 1905 he moved to Moscow. During World War I he made many military-themed colour pastels, and after the Russian Revolution he became one of the first political propaganda poster artists. In 1921 he repatriated to Latvia.

Auguste Edouart specialised in silhouette portraits, taking full-length likenesses in profile by cutting out black paper with scissors. Born in Dunkerque, he left France and settled in London, where he began his career making portraits from hair. He turned to silhouettes in 1825. After touring England for fifteen years, he arrived in Edinburgh in 1829 and made some 5,000 likenesses there in three years. He travelled in the United States for about ten years. Later he returned to France and worked on smaller silhouettes, including one of Victor Hugo.

Battista Dossi spent nearly his entire career in the service of the court of Ferrara, where he worked with his older brother Dosso Dossi. It is believed that Battista worked in Raphael's studio in Rome from 1517 to 1520. He was an Italian painter of the Ferrara School, also known as Battista de Luteri. Camillo Filippi was among his students. He died in 1548.

Colin Campbell Cooper painted architecture, especially skyscrapers in New York City, Philadelphia and Chicago. An avid traveler, he also painted European and Asian landmarks as well as landscapes and portraits. He studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts under Thomas Eakins and at the Académie Julian. He was elected a member of the National Academy of Design in 1912 and won the gold medal for oil painting at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in 1915. He taught art at Drexel University and served as dean of painting at the Santa Barbara Community School of Arts.

Domenico Corvi worked in Rome in an early Neoclassic style, between the late Rococo of Pompeo Batoni and the incipient Neoclassicism of Anton Raphael Mengs. Born in Viterbo, he moved to Rome to work under Francesco Mancini. In 1750 he won first prize at the Accademia di San Luca, and it elected him a full member in 1756, when he probably submitted his Nativity. Its atmospheric light and tender emotions show Corrado Giaquinto's early influence. That same year he returned to Viterbo to help decorate the church of the Gonfalone.

Filippo Napoletano, whose real name was Filippo Teodoro di Liagno, made landscape and genre scenes and also drawings and etchings of unusual subjects, such as exotic soldiers and animal skeletons. He was born in Rome but moved as a child to Naples, where he began his career. Around 1614 he moved back to Rome, where Flemish landscape painters such as Paul Bril and Adam Elsheimer influenced him. In 1617 Cosimo II de' Medici summoned him to Florence, where he worked closely with Jacques Callot as court painter.

Frans Ykens is mainly known for flower pieces and fruit still lifes, but he also painted banquet pieces and larger game pieces. He was baptized in Antwerp in 1601. At fourteen he began his artistic study with his uncle Osias Beert, one of the earliest painters to specialize in still lifes. In 1615 he also studied under the history painter Lucas Floquet the Elder, who later became his father-in-law. According to a statement he made in 1641, he had travelled twelve years earlier to Provence, where he stayed in Aix-en-Provence and Marseille.

Walter Ufer is best known for scenes of Native American life, particularly of the Pueblo Indians. He was born in Germany and moved with his family to Louisville, Kentucky in 1880. After an apprenticeship as a lithographer, he went to Europe as a travelling journeyman and trained in Hamburg and Dresden. Back in America he worked as a printer in Chicago and taught school, later took classes in fine arts, and in 1911 returned to Munich for further study. In 1914 he travelled to Taos. There he became one of the Taos Ten.

Georg Dionysius Ehret began his working life as a gardener's apprentice near Heidelberg, and his father was a gardener and competent draughtsman. His first illustrations were made in collaboration with Carl Linnaeus and George Clifford in 1735 and 1736. Clifford was a wealthy Dutch banker and governor of the Dutch East India Company and a keen botanist with a large herbarium. At his estate Hartecamp, south of Haarlem, Ehret and Linnaeus produced the Hortus Cliffortianus in 1738. Ehret became a leading European botanical artist.

Giovanni da Milano came from Lombardy. The earliest document puts him in Florence on 17 October 1346, under the name Johannes Jacobi de Commo, among the foreign painters living in Tuscany. His style is considered derivative of Giotto's, though Vasari misidentified him as a student of Taddeo Gaddi. The latest documentation of his career, from 1369, shows him working in Rome for Pope Urban V with Giottino and the sons of Taddeo Gaddi. He was active in Florence and Rome.

Girolamo Ferroni learned painting in Milan, then moved to Rome and trained in the workshop of Carlo Maratta. Back in Milan he painted the Dormition of St Joseph in Sant'Eustorgio. When his work as a painter was finished, he devoted himself to etching and made prints for Maratta, among them Joshua commanding the sun to stand still and Judith cutting off the head of Holofernes. With Johann Georg Seiller he contributed copperplate illustrations to Serviliano Latuada's Descrizione di Milano.

Girolamo Macchietti trained with Michele di Ridolfo. Between 1556 and 1562 he assisted Giorgio Vasari in decorating the Palazzo Vecchio, where he worked with Mirabello Cavalori. For Vasari's Studiolo of Francesco I he painted two canvases, a Jason and Medea and a Baths of Pozzuoli. He also painted an altarpiece of the Martyrdom of Saint Lawrence for Santa Maria Novella and completed a Gloria di San Lorenzo for Empoli Cathedral. He travelled to Rome and spent two years in Spain, but no works are recorded from those travels.

Henri Meunier was the son of the etcher Jean-Baptiste Meunier and the nephew of the sculptor Constantin Meunier. He received his first training in engraving in his father's workshop. After studying at the academy in Ixelles, he branched out into printmaking, poster design, graphic reporting and bookbinding. He used flat colours and thick outlines, borrowed from Japanese prints, to achieve powerful images. Many of his lithographs were published in L'Estampe Moderne, a series of 24 monthly portfolios from 1897 to 1898, printed by Champenois of Paris.

Ignazio Stern was born in Mauerkirchen in Upper Austria and became a Baroque painter in Rome. He was a pupil of Carlo Cignani in Bologna and worked in Lombardy before moving on to Rome. He painted an Annunciation for the church of the Nunziata in Piacenza. In Rome he frescoed the sacristy of San Paolino and left some oil pictures in the church of Sant'Elisabetta. He was the father of the painters Ludovico Stern and Veronica Stern. He died in Rome in 1748.

Juan García de Miranda was born without a right hand and used the stump of his arm to hold pencils and maulstick. He studied under Juan Delgado and produced chiefly devotional pictures, particularly Immaculate Conceptions, for private patrons. He was appointed to clean and restore the pictures damaged in the fire at the Alcázar, among them Las Meninas by Velázquez. He did it so well that in 1735 he became painter-in-ordinary to Philip V. From 1724 he also held, with Palomino, the post of public valuer of pictures. He was the uncle of Pedro Rodríguez de Miranda.

The Kanō school was the dominant style of painting in Japan from the late 15th century until the Meiji period, which began in 1868. By then it had divided into many branches. The Kanō family itself produced a string of major artists over several generations, and many unrelated artists trained in the school's workshops. Some artists married into the family and changed their names, and others were adopted. The school began by reflecting a renewed influence from Chinese painting. It then developed a brightly coloured, firmly outlined style for large panels decorating the castles of the nobility.

Karl Ferdinand Wimar concentrated on Native Americans in the West and the great herds of buffalo. Born in Siegburg, he immigrated to the United States at fifteen with his family, who settled in St. Louis. In 1846 he began studying painting with Leon Pomarede, and the two travelled up the Mississippi River together. In 1852 he went to the Düsseldorf Academy to study with Emanuel Leutze. An early painting of his depicts a colonial incident, the 1776 capture of Jemima Boone by a Cherokee-Shawnee raiding party.

Henry Pether belonged to the Moonlight Pethers, with his father Abraham and his older brother Sebastian, and he was famous for moonlit scenes of Britain and Venice. He was also an inventor of lamps and tiles. His father's and brother's works were often imaginary, while his own were more realistic and refined. He was noted for his control of detail, atmosphere and colouring. He generally signed his paintings, yet they are frequently attributed to his father or brother by mistake. He was born in 1800.

Louis Chéron came from a French Protestant family of artists. His father was the miniaturist and engraver Henri Chéron, and his elder sister was the painter and engraver Elisabeth-Sophie Chéron. He trained under his father and then at the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture. He won the Académie's prix de Rome twice, the first time in 1676, and on his trips to Rome he studied Raphael and Giulio Romano. After the revocation of the edict of Nantes in 1685 he left France and settled in London.

Louis Matout came from a family of modest means. An architect he met at a construction site where he was employed helped him gain admission to the École des beaux-arts in Paris. His first exhibit at the Salon came in 1833, and he kept showing there until 1879. In 1852 the Minister of Finance, Achille Fould, commissioned him to paint Dr. Ambroise Paré performing a ligature for the Grand Amphithéâtre of the Faculté de médecine, replacing a dilapidated fresco. He was known mainly for cityscapes with figures and for genre scenes, and he was also a muralist.

Maria Uhden, a German painter and printmaker, belonged to the German Expressionist movement. She was born in Coburg in 1892 and married the painter Georg Schrimpf. She died in Munich in 1918, aged only 26. Her work is in the collections of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the National Gallery of Art and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.

Marie Louveau-Rouveyre came to specialize in engraving, and her engravings included illustrations for literary works, among them some by Victor Hugo. She trained with Carolus-Duran, Auguste Laguillermie and Léopold Flameng. She was a member of the Paris Salon, and from 1873 she regularly exhibited her work there. In 1876 she presented six etchings inspired by ancient subjects. Her work was also exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. She was a French artist and engraver.

Otto Haslund is remembered in particular for his paintings of animals and children. Born in Copenhagen, he attended the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts for six years and also studied privately under Wilhelm Marstrand, Jørgen Roed and Skovgaard. He spent some time working in Vilhelm Kyhn's studio too. His early work bears traces of the Danish Golden Age approach, thanks to his friendship with Pietro Krohn, a nephew of Christen Købke. Haslund belonged to a group of artists who tried to maintain the traditional Danish approach as new styles arrived. Lundbye inspired his sensitive pictures of animals.

Ren Xiong belonged to the Shanghai School and became known for a bold, innovative style that strongly influenced it and later modern Chinese painting. He was born in Xiaoshan, Zhejiang. After leaving his teacher, he travelled to various cities and made a living through painting. In Hangzhou his fellow townsman Lu Yeshan supported him, and his portraits gained recognition. He copied the stone engravings of the Sixteen Arhats by Guanxiu at the Shengyin Temple on Gushan Island. Zhou Xian admired his work and invited him to Fanhu Cottage.

René-Xavier Prinet's father, an imperial prosecutor who painted as a hobby, supported his wish to study art and sent him to Louis Charles Timbal, a well-known church painter. The family lived on rue Bonaparte, a stone's throw from the École des beaux-arts. Prinet was born in Vitry-le-François into a family of notables from Franche-Comté, and his brother Gaston was a diplomat. Through his maternal grandmother he is related to the court painters Hubert Drouais and François-Hubert Drouais. He worked as a painter and illustrator.

Richard Morris Hunt designed the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty and the entrance façade and Great Hall of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Fifth Avenue building. He also designed many Fifth Avenue mansions, since destroyed. His Biltmore Estate near Asheville, North Carolina, is America's largest private house. He built elaborate summer cottages in Newport, Rhode Island, for the social elite of the Gilded Age. He was born in Brattleboro, Vermont, the son of the lawyer and congressman Jonathan Hunt.

Richard Ranft, born in Plainpalais, began studying painting and drawing in Geneva under Eugène Étienne Sordet, who taught him landscape painting. He then moved to Paris, where he learned engraving from the sculptor Augustin-Alexandre Dumont. Ranft created many lithographed plates, including posters, and etchings, while continuing to paint landscapes. In Paris he was elected a full member of the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts, and he exhibited regularly in its Salons. Gustave Kahn paid tribute to him in the Mercure de France a few weeks after his death in 1931.

As a boy, William Logsdail earned money by guiding visitors up the central tower of Lincoln Cathedral, where his father was a verger. He was born in the Close, one of seven children. At the Lincoln School of Art he first showed an aptitude for architecture. He is notable for his realistic scenes of London and Venice and for his plein air style. He exhibited at the Royal Academy, the Royal Society of British Artists and the Grosvenor Gallery.

Philip Wilson Steer made his name with sea and landscape paintings, which made him a leading figure in the Impressionist movement in Britain. In time he turned to a more traditional English style, clearly influenced by John Constable and Turner, and spent more time painting in the countryside than on the coast. He was born in Birkenhead, the son of a portrait painter and art teacher. When he was three, the family moved to Whitchurch near Monmouth. As a painting tutor at the Slade School of Art for many years, he influenced generations of young artists.

Simone Pignoni apprenticed with Fabrizio Boschi, then with Domenico Passignano, and finally with Francesco Furini. He is best known for a style reminiscent of the morbidly sensual Furini. In his self-portrait of around 1650, he depicts himself building up a plump naked female from a skeleton. The biographer Baldinucci called him an imitator of Furini's licentious inventions. His pupil Giovanni Camillo Sagrestani recorded a fuller biography, describing him as endowed with a bizarre and amenable intelligence. Late in life he apparently turned pious.

Zacharie Astruc was one of the first to recognize Manet's talent, befriending him in the 1850s. As an art critic, writing mainly between 1859 and 1872, he strongly defended Courbet. He also defended Monet, Whistler, Carolus-Duran, Fantin-Latour and Alphonse Legros. The art historian Michael Fried wrote that Astruc spoke for Manet's generation more than any other writer. He took part in the First Impressionist Exhibition of 1874. He also sculpted and wrote poems.

Leonardus Temminck became best known as a painter of miniature portraits. He was the son of Anthony Temminck and took painting lessons from Benjamin Samuel Bolomey. In The Hague he played a leading role in the painters' world, as head of the Confrerie Pictura and director of the Haagsche Teekenacademie. Several of his miniatures are in the Rijksmuseum, and his miniature of Prince Willem V belongs to the collection of the House of Orange-Nassau foundation in The Hague. He married in The Hague in 1777.

Adrian Schleich was the son of the copper engraver Johann Karl Schleich, inspector of the topographical bureau, and the father of the landscape painter Robert Schleich. He studied from November 1824 at the Royal Academy of Arts in Munich under Samuel Amsler. He made copper and steel engravings after designs by Wilhelm von Kaulbach, Engelbert Seibertz and others, and he also copied paintings by Raphael. He worked as well for the geographical publishing house of the Bibliographisches Institut in Hildburghausen.

Étienne Parrocel, called Le Romain, belonged to a successful dynasty of artists that produced fourteen painters over six generations. Born in Avignon in 1696, he was the son of Ignace Jacques Parrocel. He was a pupil of the Carthusian brother Gabriel Imbert and of his uncle Pierre, who took him to Rome around 1717 to study with his cousins Pierre Ignace and Joseph François. Étienne stayed in Rome until his death and Italianised his first name, which is why he was called Le Romain. His first patron, Pierre Guérin de Tencin, ordered a painting from him in 1724.

Born Moses Samuel Loewe in Königsberg, Johann Michael Siegfried Lowe became a Prussian portraitist and miniature painter who also made engravings. He studied at the Berlin Academy from 1770 to 1774 under Blaise Nicolas Le Sueur and Daniel Chodowiecki, and in Dresden under Giovanni Battista Casanova and Anton Graff. After a study trip to Venice he went to Saint Petersburg, where he is said to have painted Empress Catherine II several times and where the academy's records document him until 1788. His many portraits include August von Kotzebue, Moses Mendelssohn and Immanuel Kant.

Paul Balluriau is best known as a caricaturist and illustrator. He worked for periodicals such as L'Assiette au beurre, Le Rire, Le Journal and Fin de siècle. Together with Steinlen, he was one of the main contributors to Gil Blas illustré, and he illustrated many books and made a few posters. He also contributed to song collections and sheet music, such as Paul Delmet's Chansons du Quartier latin. His Paris studio was at 49 boulevard Saint-Marcel.

Erasmus Quellinus the Younger was one of the closest collaborators of Rubens in the 1630s. After Rubens died in 1640, he became one of the most successful painters in Flanders. He was born in Antwerp, the son of the sculptor Erasmus Quellinus I, and his brothers Artus and Hubertus were a sculptor and an engraver. He was a prolific draughtsman who made designs for official celebrations, for local publishers and for sculptures and wall hangings made in local workshops. He also painted history, portrait, battle and animal subjects.

Jean-André Rixens paid for his early art tuition by painting commercial signs and making copies of artworks. His father was a master shoemaker in Saint-Gaudens. In 1866 his painting The Death of Alcibiades earned him a scholarship from the City of Toulouse, which let him enroll at the École des beaux-arts de Paris to study with Adolphe Yvon. While there he worked for Goupil & Cie on reproductions of famous works. He later joined Gérôme's studio. His first attempt at the Prix de Rome in 1870 failed, but in 1873 he won second prize.

Jean-Damascène Sallusti served as a court painter to the Qianlong Emperor in China, alongside Giuseppe Castiglione and Ignatius Sichelbart. With them he helped create the Emperor's Battle Copper Prints, which commemorate the Ili campaign. An Italian Augustinian and later a Jesuit, he was appointed, somewhat controversially, Bishop of Beijing in 1778 and held that position until his death in 1781. The Cleveland Museum of Art holds his work.
